# Setup Appendix: Docker on Your Own Machine {#sec-setup .unnumbered}

@sec-containers teaches what a container is and why pinning a
base image by digest matters. This appendix is narrower and more
mundane: getting Docker itself to run at all, on the three
machines most readers actually sit down at, before any of that
chapter's content applies. A 2026 expert review of this book
named exactly this gap: no setup appendix covering Docker on
`arm64` laptops, `--platform linux/amd64` emulation and its
consequences, Windows and WSL2, or locked-down institutional
laptops, and judged that without it, 'weeks 2 to 4' of a course
built on this book are lost to installation trouble rather than
spent on the material itself. Nothing here is new reproducibility
theory; it is a checklist for the moment before the first `docker
build` succeeds.

## Apple Silicon (M-series Mac)

@sec-containers already explains the mechanism: `rocker/tidyverse`
and `rocker/verse`, the two base images this book's own Dockerfiles
build on, publish a `linux/amd64` entry only, so an Apple Silicon
Mac (an `arm64` host) has nothing native to match, and `--platform
linux/amd64` is not an optimization but the only way to get a
build at all. That section is worth reading before this one. What
follows is the practical sequence for a reader sitting at such a
machine for the first time.

1. **Confirm Docker Desktop is installed and running.** `docker
   version` should print both a `Client` and a `Server` block; a
   `Client`-only response, or a connection error, means Docker
   Desktop is not running, not merely that the command is missing.

2. **Add `--platform linux/amd64` to every build and run** against
   an image, like this book's own, that has no `arm64` entry:
   `docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t myimage .`. Omitting the
   flag against an `amd64`-only image does not silently succeed at
   native speed; it fails to resolve a matching entry at all.

3. **Expect the build to be slower, not wrong.** Docker's own
   documentation on multi-platform builds warns that QEMU
   emulation 'can be much slower than native builds,
   especially for compute-heavy tasks' [@docker2024multiplatform].
   A `renv::restore()` that compiles several packages from source
   is exactly that kind of task; budget minutes, not seconds, for
   a first build, and do not read slowness alone as a broken
   Dockerfile.

4. **Confirm emulation is actually what is happening**, rather
   than guessing from slowness alone. `docker image inspect
   myimage --format '{{.Architecture}}'` reports the architecture
   of the image that was actually pulled or built; `amd64` on an
   Apple Silicon host confirms QEMU emulation is in play. The
   build log itself also names the platform at the top of each
   stage (`[linux/amd64 ...]`) when `--platform` was passed
   explicitly.

## Windows with WSL2

This book's images are Linux-based, and Docker Desktop on Windows
runs them through the **WSL2 backend**, not through Hyper-V alone
and not through Windows containers, which target Windows-native
images this book never builds. Docker's own current documentation
describes the setup directly (opened 2026-10-12): WSL2 itself must
be installed and the Docker Desktop setting **Use WSL 2 based
engine** enabled under Settings > General (on by default on
systems that support it); a specific Linux distribution is then
enabled for Docker integration under Settings > Resources > WSL
Integration, which is on by default for the default distribution
[@dockerdesktopwsl2024]. Installing WSL2 itself, if it is not
already present, is a single elevated command from Windows:
`wsl --install`, per Microsoft's own documentation
[@mswslinstall2024].

The gotcha that costs real time is where the project's files
live. Microsoft's own guidance is explicit: for the fastest
performance when working from a Linux command line, store files
in the WSL Linux filesystem (`/home/<user>/project`), not on a
mounted Windows drive accessed through `/mnt/c/...`, which the
same document calls out as measurably slower [@mswslfiles2024].
A repository cloned from inside Windows Explorer or PowerShell,
then opened from a WSL2 terminal only by crossing the `/mnt/c`
mount, pays this cost on every file Docker touches during a
build. The fix is to run `git clone` from inside the WSL2
terminal itself, so the repository lands under the Linux
filesystem from the start, not to move a Windows-cloned copy
afterward.

A second, quieter hazard travels with the same mount boundary:
line endings. Git on Windows commonly checks out text files with
CRLF line endings by default (`core.autocrlf=true`), while this
book's shell scripts, Dockerfiles, and R scripts assume LF, the
Linux convention a container's shell expects. A script that
looks identical in an editor can fail inside a container with an
`exec format error` or a shebang that silently does not match,
because a trailing `\r` is part of the first line's interpreter
path as far as the kernel is concerned. Cloning inside WSL2's own
filesystem, where Git's Linux default is LF, avoids this
entirely; cloning on the Windows side and later copying into WSL2
does not.

## Locked-down institutional laptops

A reader with no administrator rights cannot install Docker
Desktop at all, a constraint the same expert review named by
name as common and often treated as an afterthought in course
materials. This is not a Docker problem to work around locally;
it is an infrastructure gap to route around, in roughly
increasing order of how much it is worth asking for:

- **A cloud-hosted development environment.** @sec-backends
  already covers GitHub Codespaces, built on the Development
  Containers specification [@devcontainers], as a way to open a
  pinned environment in an editor without installing anything
  locally beyond a browser or a thin client; it requires no local
  Docker Desktop at all, because the container runs on GitHub's
  infrastructure, not the laptop.

- **A department-provided remote server or HPC login node,**
  reached over SSH. @sec-backends's HPC worked example already
  shows the companion half of this: Apptainer, not Docker, is the
  standard container runtime on a shared cluster, and it runs
  unprivileged, which is exactly the property that makes it
  acceptable where a locked-down laptop's Docker daemon is not.
  A reader who already has cluster access may find the
  institutional gap is already closed, just not with Docker.

- **A formal request to institutional IT**, when neither of the
  above is available. The request is answerable only if it is
  concrete: ask specifically for Docker Desktop, or, if desktop
  software cannot be approved, for Docker Engine plus the
  ability to run containers under the requester's own account
  (not merely 'Docker', which names a product family spanning
  both). An IT request phrased as 'I need Docker' is easy to
  deny or stall; one phrased as 'I need to run `docker build` and
  `docker run` as my own user, without root' is a specification
  someone can actually approve or substitute for.

## Diagnosing a failed or unexpectedly slow build

When a build fails or crawls, work through this sequence before
assuming the Dockerfile itself is wrong:

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `docker info` | Confirms Docker Desktop is actually running and reachable; also reports the server's architecture. |
| `docker version` | Separates client-only output (Desktop not running) from a full client-and-server response. |
| Is `--platform` set, and does the base image need it? | An `amd64`-only base on an `arm64` host needs the flag explicitly; a missing flag there is a pull failure, not a slow build. |
| Docker Desktop's allotted disk and memory (Settings > Resources) | A build that stalls rather than errors often has hit a memory or disk ceiling Docker Desktop itself enforces, independent of the host machine's total resources. |
| Is the project under `/mnt/c` on WSL2, or on Windows' own filesystem? | Either one is the likely source of a build that is slow specifically on Windows and not elsewhere; moving the clone inside WSL2's Linux filesystem is the fix. |

On the machine this book was written on (Apple Silicon, Docker
Desktop with the `desktop-linux` context), `docker version`
reports a `darwin/arm64` client against a `linux/arm64` server
(verified, run 2026-10-12); a reader instead passing
`--platform linux/amd64`, as this book's own Dockerfile requires,
would see the pulled or built image itself report `amd64` under
`docker image inspect`, even though the daemon underneath is
`arm64`, which is the signature of emulation working as intended
rather than a misconfiguration.
